text: Over the next twenty-three videos, you're building one complete reporting platform for a fictional retailer: Riverside Outfitters. Fourteen stores, one warehouse, a point-of-sale system that dumps a CSV every night — and no real reporting beyond a spreadsheet somebody rebuilds by hand every Monday.

By the end, you'll have a SQL Server warehouse, an SSIS package that loads it automatically every night, an SSRS report every store manager opens each morning, and a Power BI dashboard the VP of Operations checks before her first meeting.
But this video doesn't start with a table, or a single line of SQL. Every real BI project starts the same way: with a meeting.

Riverside's VP of Operations is about to tell you she needs 'better reporting.' That sentence sounds like a requirement. It isn't — it's a symptom. Your job is to turn it into something testable: a specific grain, a specific audience, a precise definition of a word as simple as 'sale.'

In the meeting you're about to sit in on, one answer matters more than all the others: asked whether a sale counts before or after returns, she doesn't know. Catching that gap in a conversation is free. Catching it after the warehouse is built costs a schema change.
Watch for the trap hiding inside her request, too: automate exactly what the existing spreadsheet already does, and you've automated a workaround — not solved the actual problem.

What you'll walk away with is a one-page requirements brief, confirmed in writing, that every later decision — the warehouse's grain, the refresh schedule, what lands in SSRS versus Power BI — traces straight back to.
That's what separates a BI developer who understands the business from one who just knows the tools. Let's sit in on the meeting.
